title: Transparent queue hedging and graceful timeout requeue controller
author: Maya Patel
description: Motivation: Continuous-batcher latency outliers under bursty arrival patterns were traced to long-lived queue slots where a single request's timeout or slow kernel execution blocked downstream fairness heuristics. This PR introduces a transparent hedging layer and a controlled timeout-requeue controller to reduce tail latency and prevent starvation of small/short requests without sacrificing batching efficiency. Design summary: 1) Hedge windows: allow opportunistic speculative re-dispatch of a minimal shadow request to an alternate worker if a slot's in-flight time exceeds a dynamic threshold computed from recent service-time histograms. The hedge is lightweight and only re-routes a compact probe that does not warm full KV cache, avoiding double-KV pin storms. 2) Timeout-requeue controller: when a request's soft timeout is hit, instead of immediate hard-drop we re-enqueue with decayed priority and a backoff epoch counter. Requeued requests carry a hint that disables KV-prefetch for the first reattempt to reduce re-warm cost. 3) Fairness budget accounting: introduce per-tenant short-term credits so repeated hedging or requeues do not starve other tenants; credits decay over a short epoch to recover throughput fairness. 4) Kernel-aware admission: tie hedging thresholds to kernel selection signals so requests predicted to trigger slow kernels (long context or sampling-heavy decoding) are more likely to get early hedges, preventing single slow kernels from causing batch-wide stalls. Implementation notes: changes touch the continuous batcher coordinator, queue admission logic, KV cache manager, and kernel selector hint paths. The controller uses streaming metrics to compute a sliding 95th percentile service-time and derives a hedge threshold = max(min_threshold, percentile * multiplier) with sane defaults for production. Tests: unit tests for hedging state transitions and requeue backoff, integration tests that simulate microbursts with mixed short/long requests, and a new starvation regression that verifies small requests no longer exceed 2x median latency on heavy long-request load. Performance results: on canary with 32 GPU workers and mixed workload, P95 generation latency dropped 18-26% depending on model family, P99 improved 12-18%, median throughput dropped under 2% in the worst case. Safety and rollout: feature guarded behind runtime flags and default-off for Dedicated customers; rollout phased with canary followed by region rollouts. Backwards compatibility: new requeue hint is additive and ignored by older agents. Related: addresses regressions observed in ENG-9143 and complements earlier batching improvements by reducing long-tail impact on fairness. Follow-ups: telemetry dashboard panels for hedging incidents and a separate PR to add an operator knob for hedge aggressiveness.
